description:
We are a multidisciplinary team passionate about sustainability, environmental monitoring, and technology-driven solutions. Our skills span data science, machine learning, engineering, geospatial analysis, and web development.

Through Ignisensing Analytics, we combine NASA satellite observations, predictive modeling, and interactive visualizations to improve historical fire monitoring, haze awareness, and disaster preparedness across Southeast Asia.
summary:
Ignisensing Analytics transforms over two decades of NASA FIRMS observations into a comparable historical fire-activity record for Indonesia (2003–present). MODIS and VIIRS have different detection capabilities, making raw trends misleading. We cleaned 8.9 million hotspot records, filtered persistent heat sources, and combined LightGBM with a conversion-ratio model to generate VIIRS-equivalent estimates. Leave-one-year-out validation achieved approximately 6% typical annual error.

Our free dashboard integrates an interactive activity calendar, geographical fire map, historical analysis, provincial watchlist, CSV exports, and haze outlooks using Open-Meteo and Copernicus CAMS. These tools support researchers, emergency managers, and communities in understanding seasonal patterns, unusual activity, and potential haze conditions.

Developed using Python, pandas, scikit-learn, LightGBM, JavaScript, Leaflet, Chart.js, GitHub, Vercel, Figma, and Claude Code, our approach prioritizes scientific comparability, accessibility, and transparency. Future development includes Southeast Asian haze coverage, peatland mapping, and ground-station validation to strengthen evidence-based preparedness and environmental decision-making.
details:
Project Overview and Problem

Ignisensing Analytics is a free, interactive platform that transforms more than two decades of NASA satellite fire observations into a consistent historical record of fire activity across Indonesia, from 2003 to the present.

Indonesia faces recurring vegetation and peatland fires that generate transboundary haze, affecting public health, ecosystems, and economic activity across Southeast Asia. Reliable historical information is essential for understanding seasonal patterns, identifying unusual activity, and supporting preparedness.

However, comparing satellite fire observations across decades presents a major scientific challenge. NASA's MODIS sensor detects fires at approximately 1 km resolution, while VIIRS provides finer 375 m observations. Their different detection capabilities mean that raw hotspot counts cannot be directly compared. Simply combining their records creates an artificial increase in reported activity around 2012, when VIIRS observations became available.

Scientific Methodology and Innovation

Our team developed a harmonization pipeline to address this problem.

We processed approximately 8.9 million NASA FIRMS hotspot records, applying consistent confidence filtering, vegetation-related detection criteria, and masking procedures to reduce contamination from volcanoes, gas flares, and other persistent industrial heat sources.

The cleaned observations were organized into 0.25° geographical grid cells across Indonesia.

Using the overlapping MODIS–VIIRS observation period from 2012 to 2026, we developed a model that converts MODIS fire-detection counts into VIIRS-equivalent estimates.

The final harmonization approach combines a conversion-ratio model with LightGBM. Leave-one-year-out validation produced approximately 6% typical annual aggregate error, supporting comparisons across satellite generations.

This approach addresses a critical problem: apparent changes in hotspot activity may reflect improvements in satellite detection rather than actual changes in fire activity.

Our analysis illustrates this distinction. While raw satellite observations suggest a 3.4-fold increase, the harmonized record indicates that average activity during 2013–2025 was approximately 31% lower than during 2003–2011, under the project's existing comparison methodology.

Platform Functionality

Ignisensing Analytics translates the harmonized record into accessible visualizations and analytical tools.

Activity Calendar: An interactive year-by-month heatmap allows users to explore historical fire activity, compare raw and harmonized observations, identify seasonal patterns, and examine deviations from historical monthly medians.

Fire Map: A geographical visualization displays fire activity across Indonesia using 0.25° grid cells. Users can investigate spatial concentrations, select geographical areas, and examine historical activity. Recurrence-oriented exploration can help identify locations with repeated recorded activity where supported by the available data.

Historical Analysis: Long-term visualizations help users investigate annual trends, exceptional historical periods, and the differences between MODIS, VIIRS, and harmonized observations.

Priority Watchlist: Provincial comparisons help disaster-management agencies, land managers, and policymakers identify regions showing unusual historical activity. The platform covers 34 provinces in its historical geographical dataset and provides explainable screening indicators rather than official emergency-risk classifications.

Haze Outlook: A complementary feature integrates NASA FIRMS near-real-time detections with Open-Meteo meteorological forecasts and Copernicus CAMS atmospheric data. It provides experimental haze-related indicators for locations including Singapore and Kuala Lumpur, supporting awareness of potential smoky conditions.

Data Access and Accessibility: CSV downloads support further research and analysis. The interface is designed for desktop and mobile use, with consideration for keyboard navigation, screen readers, and accessible visual presentation.

Intended Benefits and Impact

Ignisensing Analytics is designed for emergency preparedness professionals, provincial disaster agencies, environmental authorities, researchers, land managers, and communities.

By making historical fire activity easier to interpret, the platform can support:

  • Identification of unusual seasonal fire activity.
  • Geographical screening of repeatedly affected areas.
  • Evidence-informed monitoring and preparedness planning.
  • Investigation of potential priorities for peatland restoration and community fire patrols.
  • Long-term environmental research and post-incident evaluation.
  • Greater awareness of haze-related conditions affecting communities across Southeast Asia.

The platform does not replace official fire warnings, ground observations, or operational emergency-response systems. Instead, it provides accessible historical evidence and complementary atmospheric information to support further investigation and preparedness.

Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using publicly available satellite and atmospheric data alongside open-source software and AI-assisted development tools.

Data sources: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS, NASA GIBS imagery, Open-Meteo meteorological forecasts, and Copernicus CAMS atmospheric information.

Scientific processing: Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, and LightGBM.

Frontend and visualization: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Leaflet, and Chart.js.

Development and deployment: GitHub for version control, Vercel for hosting, Figma and Miro for design and planning, and Claude Code for AI-assisted implementation.

The project was developed using conventional laptops, without specialized hardware.

Creativity and Development Considerations

Ignisensing Analytics is innovative because it addresses the scientific comparability of satellite observations before presenting long-term fire trends.

Rather than combining raw datasets and potentially misleading users, the platform applies documented filtering and harmonization methods to construct a more consistent historical record.

Its design integrates temporal, geographical, and provincial analysis within one accessible application.

The team also considered model validation, observation uncertainty, incomplete periods, source provenance, and the distinction between satellite detections and individual physical fires.

These considerations help prevent users from misinterpreting changes caused by satellite technology as changes in environmental conditions.

Future Development

Future improvements include expanding haze outlook coverage across Southeast Asia, incorporating verified peatland and environmental datasets, and validating atmospheric forecasts against ground-based monitoring stations.

Additional work will focus on improving geographical interpretation, evaluating model performance, and collaborating with potential institutional users.

Our goal is to make scientifically comparable fire information more accessible, helping communities and institutions make better-informed preparedness and environmental management decisions.
